introduction-is-docker-secure-enough.core: Standard runc containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability or container escape can compromise the node and other tenants. For trusted, well-hardened workloads this is acceptable. For untrusted or multi-tenant code (customer plugins, CI jobs, user notebooks), stronger isolation via sandboxed runtimes is prudent.

first_principles.problem: A platform runs arbitrary customer code in standard containers next to sensitive internal services.
truths: The kernel is a shared attack surface.
Hardening reduces but doesn't remove risk.

analogy.title: Office cubicles versus locked labs
analogy.story: Cubicles are fine for colleagues, but strangers with unknown chemicals need a sealed lab.
analogy.breaks: Labs are physically sealed; sandboxes reduce, not eliminate, escape risk.

check.q: When are standard runc containers insufficient isolation?
check.a: When running untrusted or multi-tenant code where a kernel escape would expose other tenants or the host.

sandboxed-runtimes-gvisor-and-kata-conta.core: gVisor (runsc) runs a user-space kernel (Sentry) that implements Linux syscalls, so container syscalls hit gVisor rather than the host kernel, giving a much smaller attack surface with modest memory overhead but some syscall and I/O performance cost. Kata Containers run each Pod in a lightweight VM (QEMU, Cloud Hypervisor or Firecracker) with its own guest kernel for hardware-enforced isolation, with higher startup and memory overhead.

first_principles.problem: A team must choose between gVisor and Kata for untrusted workloads.
truths: Hardware virtualisation is a strong boundary.
Both have compatibility and performance trade-offs.
derivation: **gVisor**: lightweight, syscall-heavy apps slower, some syscalls unsupported.
**Kata**: VM isolation, needs nested virt or bare metal, more overhead.

analogy.title: An interpreter versus a separate room
analogy.story: gVisor translates every request through an interpreter; Kata gives each guest their own soundproof room.
analogy.breaks: Interpreters can be fast for short talks; gVisor overhead grows with syscall intensity.

example.title: Benchmark snapshot
flow: Syscall-heavy (many small file ops): gVisor slower
Startup: runc 0.3 s, gVisor 0.5 s, Kata 1–2 s

check.q: What does Kata Containers use to isolate Pods?
check.a: A lightweight virtual machine with its own guest kernel per Pod.

runtimeclass-the-selector-mechanism.core: RuntimeClass is a cluster-scoped object mapping a name to a CRI handler configured on nodes (runsc, kata-qemu, kata-fc). It can declare overhead (extra CPU and memory the sandbox consumes, added to Pod requests for scheduling and quotas) and scheduling constraints (nodeSelector, tolerations) so Pods land only where that runtime exists.

first_principles.problem: Sandboxed Pods are scheduled onto nodes without gVisor installed and fail to start.
truths: Not all nodes have every runtime.
Pods need a simple way to choose.

analogy.title: Labelled service counters
analogy.story: Each counter offers a specific service, and signs direct customers only to counters that offer it.
analogy.breaks: Counters can be added instantly; nodes need runtime installation first.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Handler available and selectable by name.

code.text:
# /etc/containerd/config.toml
[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.runsc]
  runtime_type = "io.containerd.runsc.v1"
# then:
# kind: RuntimeClass, handler: runsc, scheduling.nodeSelector: {sandbox: gvisor}

check.q: Why declare overhead in a RuntimeClass?
check.a: So the sandbox's extra CPU and memory are added to Pod requests for accurate scheduling and quota accounting.

assigning-pods-to-runtimes.core: Pods opt into a runtime with spec.runtimeClassName. Enforce usage with admission policies (Kyverno, Gatekeeper or CEL) so tenant namespaces must use the sandbox class, keep sandbox nodes tainted and dedicated, and verify the runtime by inspecting the node (crictl inspect) or dmesg inside gVisor. Without a runtimeClassName, the default runtime (runc) applies.

first_principles.problem: Developers forget runtimeClassName, so untrusted Pods run on runc anyway.
derivation: **Taint** sandbox nodes; tolerations come from the RuntimeClass.

analogy.title: A rule that all visitors must use the visitor entrance
analogy.story: Guards check badges so nobody slips in through the staff door.
analogy.breaks: Guards can be distracted; admission policies check every Pod.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: No tenant Pod can run outside the sandbox.

code.text:
apiVersion: kyverno.io/v1
kind: ClusterPolicy
metadata: {name: require-gvisor-in-tenants}
spec:
  validationFailureAction: Enforce
  rules:
  - name: tenant-pods-use-gvisor
    match: {any: [{resources: {kinds: [Pod], namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {tenant: "true"}}}}]}
    validate:
      message: "Tenant Pods must use runtimeClassName gvisor"
      pattern: {spec: {runtimeClassName: gvisor}}

check.q: What runtime does a Pod use if runtimeClassName is omitted?
check.a: The node's default runtime handler (typically runc).
